source.title: Short term use of oral corticosteroids and related harms among adults in the United States: population based cohort study
source.source_type: retrospective population-based cohort study with self-controlled case series

extraction_metadata.scope_note: The primary article and its nine-page supplementary appendix were extracted as one source packet. Bibliographic entries were not atomized. All model-extracted atoms remain needs_review.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to characterize short-term oral corticosteroid prescribing and quantify associated acute sepsis, venous thromboembolism, and fracture events.
The investigators used a retrospective population-based cohort design with a self-controlled case series analysis.

source_anchor.paragraph: Study design and population; Self controlled case series

atoms.canonical_statement: The data source was the Clinformatics DataMart, a nationwide private health insurance claims database with outpatient pharmacy claims.
Eligible participants were adults aged 18-64 years who were continuously enrolled from 1 January 2012 through 31 December 2014 and had continuous enrollment during 2011.
The cohort excluded 293,456 people for any oral corticosteroid use during 2011.
The cohort excluded 102,243 people for exclusive use of non-oral corticosteroids or oral budesonide.

atoms.canonical_statement: The cohort analysis calculated adverse-event incidence rates per 1000 person-years and cumulative 5-90 day risks after a clinic visit.
The self-controlled case series compared events during days 5-30 and 31-90 after prescription with the reference period 5-180 days before prescription.
A four-day window around the prescription fill date was excluded from the primary self-controlled analysis to reduce overlap between drug receipt and adverse events.
Only the first event for each outcome was counted, and people with the corresponding adverse event in 2011 were excluded.
Patients admitted to hospital within 14 days before the corticosteroid prescription were excluded from the self-controlled analysis.
Fixed conditional Poisson regression estimated incidence rate ratios, with outcome-specific adjustment for time-varying concomitant drug classes.
The investigators tested effect modification by age, sex, and race using interaction terms.

Matched-diagnosis between-person analyses compared 30-day event rates after a clinic visit among patients with the same diagnoses who did and did not receive corticosteroids, adjusted for age, sex, and race.
The self-controlled analysis was repeated after stratification by respiratory versus musculoskeletal indications.
A sensitivity analysis excluded patients using concomitant non-oral corticosteroids.
A sensitivity analysis expanded the prescription-date exclusion window from four days to seven days.
Analyses used SAS 9.4 and Stata/MP 14.1 with two-sided tests and alpha 0.05.

atoms.canonical_statement: The cohort contained commercially insured adults and excluded people older than 64 years, limiting generalizability to older adults and other insurance populations.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: Prescription indications and prescribing specialties could be misclassified because claims were linked to the diagnosis closest to the prescription date.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: Very low corticosteroid doses were infrequent, so the study could not adequately assess adverse-event risks at those doses.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: The study evaluated only three acute adverse-event categories and counted only hospital admissions for sepsis, so other corticosteroid harms were not measured.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: Time-varying factors other than measured concomitant drugs could differ between risk and baseline periods, leaving residual confounding in the self-controlled analysis.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: The self-controlled case series assumptions and restriction to first events could yield conservative incidence rate ratios if prior events influenced subsequent drug use.

source_anchor.paragraph: Strengths and limitations of this study

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that short-term oral corticosteroids were frequently prescribed for common conditions and were associated with increased rates of sepsis, venous thromboembolism, and fracture.
The authors stated that the adverse-event association was present even at relatively low corticosteroid doses.
The authors called for studies to identify optimal corticosteroid use and to test whether treatment alternatives could improve patient safety.

Funding included a US Department of Veterans Affairs career development award, University of Michigan support, a W K Kellogg Foundation grant, and University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation support; the funders had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or report writing.

The authors declared no support from any organization for the submitted work, no relevant financial relationships in the previous three years, and no other relationships or activities that could appear to influence the work.
The article states that no additional data are available.
The University of Michigan institutional review board approved the study and waived informed consent.
